I desire to associate
myself with my hon. friends on this side who have congratulated the minister on the full and interesting statement he has made.
I am glad to hear him saying a good word of the College of Agriculture at Truro, which began in a small way about 1685 or 1886.
I remember the beginning of it very well; it began as an attachment to the provincial normal school. At first it was a sort of agricultural department in the normal school. Later on buildings were erected; a farm was purchased, and my successors in office have developed it in a large way and I am glad to know that the college is doing excellent work. I am pleased to learn that an illustration farm will be located in Cape Breton. Even in a comparatively small province like Nova Scotia, we speak of East and West, and when the time came for the location of the School of Agriculture a little difficulty arose in connection with the location of it. The most attractive farm land in the province from some viewpoints was the Annapolis valley, and there was a strong desire to locate the institution there. It was, however, felt that an experimental farm should not be located at the most attractive point, but that a location should be. selected where the soil was of average quality, similar to that of the farms of the people it was intended to reach. Since the location of the provincial farm at Truro, the Dominion Government have located one at Kentville in the West. If the minister is able to increase the number of illustration stations, they would be very welcome. Did he mention where these were in Nova Scotia, other than the Kentville one?	.
There is one at Nappan.
That is a branch of the Ottawa institution.
So is Kentville.
I understand the Kentville farm is quite a small farm.
It is quite a large farm; I was there last fall.

Are there any more
besides those at Nappan and Kentville?
In Nova Scotia ten illustration stations are being planned for at the present time.

I should like to make a suggestion to my hon. friend. If these illustration stations mean only comparatively small expenditures, although most of

my constituents are not farmers, a large number being fishermen and lumbermen, there is a large agricultural section in North [DOT] Queen's country, adjoining the county of Annapolis. This is an excellent agricultural district, and I should be glad if the minister, in selecting the locations of these illustration stations, would bear in mind the attractions and claims of that section.

I regret I was not in the Chamber when the minister was making his statement preliminary to the introduction of these Estimates. It is possible that the minister may have referred to the suggestion which I shall now offer to the committee and to the minister for what it is worth. It is well known that, under the Act of Confederation, the powers of the provinces and the Dominion in matters of agricultural administration are equal. This has led to a considerable amount of duplication in the work that is carried on by the Dominion Department of Agriculture and the various provincial departments. For instance, I know it is a fact that many of the provincial Departments of Agriculture are carrying on work similar to that done by the Federal Government through its demonstration farms. Manitoba and Alberta, I know, have illustration farms. This means a very considerable increase in the total expenditure on this class of work. If my memory serves me right, the total amount spent by the Departments of Agriculture in Canada, both federal and provincial, runs to about $7,500,000 annually, and it has occurred to me that if a better understanding could be reached with the provinces in respect to the various fields of endeavour, probably a great deal more in the way of results might be achieved from this expenditure. This duplication applies not only to demonstration and illustration farms, but to other fields of activity in agriculture. Almost all the provinces, if not all of them, have departments dealing with livestock, as well as with dairying, beekeeping, poultry raising, in all of which fields the federal department is working. The Federal Government has its officials at the experimental farms in the provinces, and there is also another set of officials under provincial control, doing similar work. I think that possibly greater efficiency, without additional expenditure, could be secured if a better understanding could be reached between the provinces and the Federal Department of Agriculture in respect to their respective fields of inquiry and endeavour. That par-

tlcularly presses upon our attention at the present time because of the great burden of taxation which this country is facing. It is a case of making our dollars go just as far as we can and if the minister by cooperation with the provinces can promote a better understanding in this regard, he will be doing a real and genuine service to agriculture in this country. I know it is perhaps difficult to do. Unfortunately in the field of agriculture, as in some other departments of our governmental service, the provinces desire to carry on their own particular inquiries, and it is often a little difficult to adjust the differences and, shall I say, perhaps the jealousies, that may exist. Nevertheless, the task is one that I think should be undertaken, and I know of no time in our history that was more opportune to undertake it than now. I offer this suggestion to the minister and the Government for what it is worth. I think if they examine it closely they will find some merit in it.

I greatly appreciate the
suggestion of the hon. member for Marquette. We realized that there was considerable duplication between, the federal and provincial Departments of Agriculture, and we called a meeting of deputy ministers about two months ago in the city of Ottawa, when the matter was very fully discussed. We have made a certain amount of progress along the line of having the different fields of endeavour more clearly defined.
I am very glad to hear it.

I was very
much interested in the statement made by the minister, and as to -its educative value I wish to endorse the suggestion of the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) that the statement should be printed and distributed as widely as possible throughout Canada. There is probably no business in Canada to-day to which the application of science brings greater results than agriculture. It is a case of knowing cause and effect. There has been great care exercised in the production of livestock, and in the selection of animals for breeding purposes, but it is only in recent years that it has been impressed on our farmers that the same care in the selection and improvement of seed brings equally good results. We know what a great benefit to the country the improvement in our wheat seed has been, and in this connection I wish to bring to the minister's attention a matter to which I referred a year ago, and that is the good work 162
that a citizen of Saskatchewan is carrying on in the improvement of wheat seed, and the great benefit it has been to agriculture in this country. This man up to the present has not been recognized by the Government for the work he has done, although I was pleased to see a few days ago that Queens University had conferred a degree upon him in recognition of the work he has done in the breeding of seed. I refer to Mr. S. Wheeler, a man who has brought credit to Canada in the breeding of seed wheat. I understand that at the present time he is working on a new seed wheat which he has developed to quite an extent, and which he names "Bobs." He is endeavouring to produce a seed that will be rust proof. It is about fifteen or sixteen years ago that rust first made its appearance in Western Canada, and since then there has been more or less rust every season. If Mr. Wheeler succeeds in producing a seed that will resist rust, it will mean a saving of millions and millions of dollars to the country. I think the Department of Agriculture .should recognize to some extent the great work this man is doing for agriculture, and should put him at all events beyond the necessity of worrying .about financial matters so far as his experiments are concerned. I thought it proper that I should again bring this matter to the attention of the minister.

The minister was kind enough to say this afternoon that he would take into serious consideration the question of providing for an increased acreage in the Experimental Farm in South Essex, at Harrow. I think the minister was there recently, and I am sure the people gathered the impression that something wras going to be done. I do not know whether the minister said so, but that is the impression the people have. The amount of $7,000 in the Estimates is very small for the upkeep of a farm in such an excellent agricultural county as Essex, and I trust the minister will see his way clear to be a little more generous in his expenditure there.

I -was not able to get down to Essex county, but the deputy minister was there. The Harrow farm, like nearly all the tobacco farms, shows a profit, so there will be that profit to expend, in addition to the $7,000. So far as the extension of work is concerned, I of course appreciate the situation that exists, and I am anxious to do everything that is .at all possible. The department is anxious to expand the experimental farm system everywhere, but



present financial conditions must be borne in mind.

May I ask the minister what provision is being made in order to meet the changing conditions that are now arising in the West, where districts which were largely, and in some cases wholly, wheat-producing are now turning their attention to stock raising and dairying? I have in mind particularly the district of Rosthern, where is situated one of the Saskatchewan farms. In this district one man is using the sunflower ensilage about which the Minister of Agriculture has spoken to-day, and I may inform the minister-for I think the fact is of some importance-that the people in that district are of the opinion that it will be wise for the Government farms to lead the way along these lines. I should therefore like to know what steps are being taken to meet the changing conditions.

In such sections as Rosthern we are establishing dairy herd systems. In that section we are starting this system, and for the farm we have -already purchased some pure-bred Holstein cattle. We shall have a barn built there as soon as possible.

My hon. friend's answer to my question a few moments ago in regard to demonstration farms is rather indefinite. He -said that he had had many requests from all over Canada. May I ask if he will take my request into serious consideration and see if he cannot do something for my riding?
I promise the hon. gentleman to take his request into serious consideration.

The minister said a moment ago that certain work would be done at Harrow, and I may be permitted to remark that whether or not experimental farms return a pecuniary profit they are entirely necessary and their establishment is perfectly justifiable. I should think that the last thing we would want to do would be to curtail the expansion of experimental farm work. I do not want any lengthy list, but can the minister inform the committee whether the principal farms !are self-sustaining? The statement has been made that so far as Western Ontario is concerned conditions are, so good that nothing more is required in the way of demonstration farms. Admitting that to be true, yet, in my opinion, a place can never be so good as not to need further development. Farm-	.	.! Lr_j 3 D
ing of every description is carried on in that locality -and I think that demonstration farms should be established there as soon as possible. I should like to know- and I think it is a matter of some interest to the people throughout the country - what percentage of the experimental farms of Canada are self-sustaining and if any revenue which may be derived from them is put back into the farms in the form of further expansion.

I was mistaken when I said that the returns went back into the farms; they are turned into the Receiver-General. The experimental farms on the whole are not profitable. From the nature of the work they carry on it is impossible that they should be profitable. For instance, many of the plots contain only one-fortieth of an acre, and every bit of work done on such a plot is done by hand. After some information of value is secured it is not immediately released. Further experimental work along the particular line is carried on for four or five years, and when we have proved beyond doubt that our information so secured is of real value then we distribute it. The mere seed or grain or roots that may be obtained from any experimental plot of such a size is not of any real profit. The real profit that is derived from such a plot consists in the information that is filed away for dissemination among the farmers of the country.
Quite so.
From a rough estimate, it is calculated that the potential value of the experimental farm system of Canada is no less than $60,000,000 a year.

I am sure that the minister must have overlooked the statement made by the hon. member for Saskatoon. I think that the work of the distinguished scientist to- whom reference has been made was spoken of last year, when there was a good deal of talk about it. We find now that the same scientist is endeavouring to produce wheat which will be rust-proof. I rather think that the minister forgot to make some reference to the observations of the hon. member for Saskatoon, and it would be a pity to let the subject go by unnoticed.

I thank the hon. member for bringing the matter to my attention. I quite recognize the ability of Mr. Seager Wheeler, and his work is just another illustration of what energy, knowledge, and application can do. Other farmers around the

district are, I think, in a position to obtain good results if they will take advantage of the opportunities at hand. Mr. Seager Wheeler is working in co-operation with our Seed Branch and all the information that can be obtained is being made use of. I am glad to receive the suggestion of the hon. member for Saskatoon that the department should recognize what Mr. Wheeler has done, and I can assure him that this matter will receive attention.

I cannot let this opportunity pass without making a plea for that part of the country from which I come, namely, the southwestern part of Saskatchewan, which is an arid district. If farming conditions in Ontario are said to be so good that they do not need experimental farms, I can assure the minister that conditions in our part of the country are the reverse and are such as to make the establishment of a farm there imperative. The district around there is 150 miles square and it is settled by as good farmers as can be found anywhere in Canada. Every dollar of our money is staked in the land and we have either to make that land profitable or walk out and leave it. If we had an experimental farm in that part of the country it would be possible, by demonstrating to the farmers the benefits to be . derived from different kinds of tilling, development along various lines, etc., then to make the land pay, and I would ask the Government to make a start this year. I do not ask them to spend a lot of monev but I would request that they make a start on an experimental farm in that district to see if they cannot help the farmers there. I know those men, for I have been with them for the last sixteen years, and I can safely say that no better class of men can be found anywhere in this Dominion., When we went out there in the Victory Loan campaign in 1918 (Swift Current was the first place in Saskatchewan to win the flag. I think it -was a remarkable achievement, and it is but right that such men who have the sand to labour under disadvantages and carry on so well should be helped as much as possible. I trust therefore that the minister will take the matter into earnest consideration and try to make a start there this year.

House again in Committee of Supply- Minister of Finance-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
.Experimental farms, $1,200,000.

Just before recess my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. 
McKenzie) succeeded in getting an assurance from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) that an illustration farm would be established in Cape Breton Island, and I must express my great satisfaction at the decision of the minister. However, when he sends his officer down there to determine the site of that farm, I would ask him not to forget to have that officer go over the most important part of the Island-from an agricultural standpoint at least-that is, the western part. If the officer is a competent man, as I have no doubt he is, I am satisfied where the site will be.

During the afternoon
we learned that the department has established a number of demonstration farms at various points throughout the greater part of Canada, but I did not hear any reference made to the district of Central Ontario. There is no agricultural college or agricultural farm between Ottawa and Guelph. The whole of that Central Ontario district is a splendid farming section, and I am sure that all that it is necessary for me to do is to direct the attention of the minister to the need for the establishment of one of these demonstration farms in the county of Peterborough.

Just before six o'clock the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Argue) had directed the attention of the minister to the need of an experimental farm in that dried-out area, as they call it, in the southwest portion of Saskatchewan and southern Alberta. I wish to emphasize as strongly as I can the need of that experimental farm. It is not a matter of local concern; a national obligation is involved. For this reason: some years ago when Hon. Frank Oliver was Minister of the Interior, the Federal Government attempted to change from a ranching district into a farming district an enormous area in that western country-as largij I should say, as the whole of the settled portion of Ontario. The Federal Department of the Interior threw thousands of farmers into that district, a district which had never been recognized as suited for farming. The result was that thousands of farmers have had to gain experience of the conditions there-conditions entirely different from those to which they had been accustomed. They have not succeeded. The country is a good country. The land is good; it is not an arid but a semi-arid district. They have almost enough rainfall to make farming a success every year, but in the absence of more than "almost enough," they have failed, in many years, all over

that district. The farmers out there are not able to do the experimenting themselves. You cannot expect a lot of pioneers to do the necessary experimenting; they have not the money. I consider it the duty of the Federal Government, therefore, who have drawn hundreds of thousands of people there, to do the experimenting which will supply these people with the information necessary to make farming a success. If a farm is established there it will undoubtedly cost a few thousand dollars, but if you thereby enable these people to carry on their operations successfully; if you can get them to grow the kind of grain which is suited to a semi-arid district-and I understand that can be done-you will make for this country millions of dollars every year. Last year, by reason of the fact that they had not this source of direction and knowledge, Canada lost millions of dollars. Can we reasonably, then, hesitate to make the necessary expenditure? I urge upon the minister that he give the proposal of the hon. member for Swift Current that attention which it deserves.

I would like to add a word or two' to what the member for East Peterborough (Mr. iSexsmith) has just said about the distribution of demonstration farms. It is true that 'the experimental farm at Guelph, for example, has been of the greatest possible benefit to our district,-not the county of Peterborough only, but to the whole district. But Guelph is a long way from Peterborough-it is considerably more than two hundred miles -and while the more energetic farmer goes there sometimes, or the more curious, it is not always possible for farmers to do themselves justice in this respect. The only place where they can obtain the necessary information, therefore, is the Experimental Farm at Ottawa. It is altogether out of reason that experimental farms Should not be more generously distributed than that. Although I am not, like my confrere, a practical farmer, I am nevertheless a theoretical farmer and a very interested farmer. I really take an intense interest in the cultivation of the land,- perhaps by other people. However, I know farmers and farming conditions fairly well, and I am convinced that nothing could be done of greater benefit to the farming community and therefore to the people generally than the placing of demonstration farms-I (would say model farms-in each county. An inspected and superintended farm that is, a farm as it ought to be, with all the equipment of a modern farm for
intensive farming-because intensive farming has to come sooner or later if farming is to be made profitable and we are to hold our own with the rest of the world-such a farm, I say, should in my humble opinion be established, or at least assisted, subsidized if you like, in each county, so that the farmers in the immediate vicinity could profit by them, and those who want to go into agricultural life might have some place close at hand where they could learn how these things should be done. Many men do not know the remedy for evil conditions which arise on their farms. They cannot afford to incur great expense in connection with them, and if there were a centre-not necessarily an expensive centre-close at hand where they might go and learn the condition of agriculture in the county in question would be improved not less than fifty per cent, I am sure, and the production accordingly. The Government cannot pay too much attention to agriculture in this respect. If my position be correct, that it is not unreasonable that there should be a local centre in each county, how really absurd is the condition when, as I say, there is no demonstration farm of any kind within a radius of two hundred miles. I hope, therefore, that the minister will note that we (are practically destitute of an agricultural centre of this kind, and that that need is one which ought to be met.

I wish to say a word on this subject, representing, as I do, one of the largest agricultural and dairying constituencies in the Dominion, and perhaps one of the best. My good friend from the constituency of Beauce (Mr. Beland) may dispute that point-he has done so on several occasions-but he has not visited South Renfrew in recent years. It will be comforting to the minister to know that I am not going to 'press a claim upon him for a model farm, an experimental farm or a demonstration farm for South Renfrew. The majority of the farms in South Renfrew are, I can assure you, Sir, model farms already, so that 'they require very little assistance along that line. The hon. members for East and West Peterborough have my sympathy, nevertheless, and I sincerely trust, in view of the fact that the need is pressing there, the minister will listen to their request and grant it as quickly as possible. I said that I came from one of the largest and best agricultural and dairying constituencies in the Dominion of Canada.
After Beauce.

I say that advisedly, notwithstanding the objection of my hon. friend (Mr. Beland). That is a habit .of his, but nevertheless the fact remains. I wish to direct the attention of the committee, and particularly of my hon. friend (Mr. Beland), to the fact that in the South Biding of Renfrew we have one of the best-watered agriculture districts in Canada. It is watered fey the river Bonnechere, which rises in Golden lake; we have also in that constituency, you will be pleased to know, in addition to all the other beauties that exist there, the Garden of Eden on one side of the town of Renfrew and the land of Goshen on the other.
Do you make maple sugar there?

We make maple sugar of the best quality, a quality that will pass the most rigid inspection of the inspectors of the Health Department. In .addition to a superior brand of maple sugar, seeing that we have such desirable spots there as the Garden of Eden and the land of Goshen, we have a land flowing practioally with milk and honey. The hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) wants to know if there is any whiskey in the South Riding of Renfrew. I am not an expert in matters of that kind, but I would not be surprised .at all if there is some of that delectable nectar also in that constituency. Speaking personally, while I have not been a farmer in recent years, most of the members in the Chamber at the present time will be surprised to learn that a man who has spent forty-five years in the business of merchandising claims that he is a farmer. The earliest years of my life were spent on a farm. I have done everything on the farm a man, even of my size, could possibly do. I have ploughed and sowed and reaped and mowed; I have done all these things in turn, erven in the old days when the reaping hook was the favoured mowing machine and the spade was the favoured plough. Therefore, I can speak with authority even on matters of that kind.
I have listened with great attention and deep interest to the excellent review of the agricultural situation as given this afternoon by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie). He made special reference to the development, by those under him in his department, of seeds and stock and farm products generally. Reference was made recently by an eminent scientist in this city -I refer tb Sir Oliver Lodge-to the unique position held by Canada in the production

of wheat. That eminent student, although up in the air sometimes in some of his ideas on life and the hereafter, occasionally takes time to investigate passing events. He had taken notice of the fact that Canada had produced the best wheat in the world, and that wheat was produced by a Canadian, a professor of the experimental farm I refer to the Marquis wheat produced by Prof. Saunders. He referred to a later development in wheat of a still better quality, now, 1 understand, passing under the name of "Bobs," and produced by a man named Seager Wheeler, also a Canadian. I congratulate the department on these developments and the progress made along these lines.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), on one point particularly, and I should like to refer to that point again, because I believe it is one worthy of special attention of the Minister of Agriculture, namely, the danger of overlapping. Joking aside, it is all very well for each county to ask for an experimental or model farm and all that sort of thing, but there are limits to the possibilities along that line, and it will be well for the minister to confer with the agricultural departments of the different provinces so that there may be no overlapping. I think the Minister of Agriculture of the Dominion Government should develop the higher part of his work and leave the other departments fo the provinces to deal with, and he should so co-operate with them as to avoid overlapping in the work attempted.
It would be interesting to make a passing reference at least to a few of the points in contrast between farm conditions in this country in the past and farm conditions as these obtain at the present moment. I trust I shall not be trespassing too much on the time of the committee by making just a passing reference to these features, and then I will give some reasons for certain suggestions I purpose making as regards the disbursement of the vote under consideration. Pioneer life in this country, as we all know, was most strenuous. The pioneers arrived here from the Old Country; they were dumped in the forest, and their first efforts would be to build a log house for a place to live in. In those days they were not surrounded by such luxuries as obtain at the present time. They were accustomed to the use of primitive instruments such as the spade, the scythe, the reaping hook, the ox-wagon, with oxen for ploughing

instead of horses. Their stock was not the class that we have to-day, it was scrub stock, and, instead of having modern machinery to separate the milk, that had all to he done by hand. The isolation, too, must have been almost intolerable in those days, almost desperate. An,d yet this hardy race of people made the wilderness blossom as the rose. 'What a difference there is in the surroundings of to-day! In almost every home in rural Ontario1 at least there are telephones; there are a daily rural mail service, motor cars, tractors, and in Western Ontario, electricity, which has developed more largely in the western part of Ontario than it has in the eastern part, but of course improvements will follow there also. The people havS modern machinery for both their homes and their farms. In the olden days, as I have already indicated, there was first the log house and then the clapboard house, but now most modern farms have brick residence with large modem barns, thoroughbred stock and all kinds of labour saving machinery for both the home and the farm.
As to what is being done by the Agricultural Department to assist in the further development of all this, I will refer to just some features that I have gathered from a publication issued by the Ontario Department of Agriculture. I refer to crop bulletin 142, which gives a great deal of general information. In spite of all this improvement, in spite of all the work that is being done by the Department of Agriculture, and in spite of the call back to the farms, that call remains unheeded, as we can easily see by reading the daily press and other reports.
One man from Pembroke, North Kenfrew, writes to the Department of Agriculture, Ontario:
There have been more sales of farms and stock and machinery this spring than in twenty years. Few people now appear to want to work on the farm.
The point I wish to make in that connection is this. The labour problem is one of the most important that confronts the farmers at the present time, and I appeal to the Minister of Agriculture to devote part of this appropriation towards assisting the farmer along these lines and try to improve conditions. Another writes:
This " hack to the land " that is being preached by men that you could not drive back to the land with a dub is all rot. There is no coming back to the land observable; it is all the other way.
Another farmer from Vespra, Simcoe county, writes:
Celibacy and childless marriages are sadly too common. How it all will end time alone can tell. I fear that the foreign element will ultimately dominate our country, and that the Canadians of the future will be of an entirely new cast.	.
That is his opinion why the farmers have difficulty in getting help. I am sorry the bon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Curriel is not in his seat. I would also like the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) to be here to take notice of that view expressed from Simcoe county.
Another farmer writes from Cornwall, Stormont county:
A number of farms have changed hands recently in this vicinity, mostly to Quebec people, who seem to stick to the soil.
That is another statement that would have been of very great interest, I am sure, to the hon. member from Frontenac, indicating trouble possibly for him to attend to.
There are other problems of the farm besides the labour problem. I think that a large part of the appropriation we are being asked to vote should be used expressly to relieve the labour situation and to give assistance in other directions. For instance large implements which cannot be purchased by individuals and which are great labour-saving devices, should be loaned by the department to farmers throughout the country, because the saving of labour is so very important at the present time. A farmer writes from Oxford, Grenville county:
There is nothing that would increase production so much in this county as drainage. If the Government could be induced to put a ditcher for underdraining into each township and let the farmers pay the running expenses it would be a godsend to this country. We have the tile very convenient.
Here is another suggestion which I think is a very important one. It has been adopted in the Old Country to assist farmers there. I would ask the minister to pay particular attention to this, from Whitby township:
Farmers who have houses for their men have all the assistance they require, but those who do not furnish houses are short of help.
I know from experience in Ireland that they had great difficulty there along the same line in days gone by, but in recent years the Government have given assistance to the farmers in the way of capital to help them build homes for their labour. I think when a farm of moderate size is able to offer the inducement to a married man and his family of a decent home with two or

three acres of land, it is of great benefit to the individual farmer, and ultimately to the whole community. It would help to bring about what we are all preaching from day to day, namely, greater production. This man has a home for his hired help and has no difficulty in obtaining all the help he requires.
The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Argue) and the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Cowan) have referred to the great need there is of assistance of the department to the farmers of the southern part of Saskatchewan. During last fall I had some experience in that province, in the constituency of Assiniboia. I saw most of the southern part' of the province during my	stay and got quite	a lot
of information about western lands and conditions generally that was of great value to me personally, and has been of great value to some of my friends in the vicinity of Renfrew who are desirous of moving out West. I found that a lot of lands out there were held by speculators. That is a rotten condition, in my opinion, and I think there should be some method of forcing that land on the market. At present the Canadian Pacific and other people are simply holding these lands for speculative purposes, and this has a tendency to keep settlers far apart, that is, there is a great distance between one settler and his next-door neighbour. That means, of course, that the schools are a considerable distance away from many of the farmers. I found, however, some very pleasant surprises in that desert land, and some very nice homes. One home I visited was that of a man who had gone out there from Tweed, Ontario, fourteen years ago and who had taken up a quarter-section of land. Later on, he acquired another quarter-section. Besides this half-section he owns one of the nicest homes I have ever seen anywhere. It was modern in every respect, with hardwood floors, hot water heating, electric light, and so forth. It was one of the greatest surprises I have'evei had. It just shows what thrift and energy on the part of an experienced man from Ontario can do, even in the not auspicious surroundings I found obtaining out there.
I might also refer to the school situation there. I was surprised and pleased to see the provision that had been made for the training and education of youth. It was one of the most pleasant things I observed possibly during my entire trip through that constituency.
Does the hon. gentleman think we are a lot of barbarians out there?
I did not expect to find the people indulge in such extravagance in the matter of schools.
Extravagance! Is that the hon. member's idea of education? Education is not extravagance.

The people evidently intended to provide the best equipment possible in the matter of education for the rising generation. In the town of Estevan, with a population of only 2,500, I saw three large public schools and a high school. I queried the necessity for such extravagance in a matter of that kind, and I was informed that most of the residents in that part of the country came out there young people, and they all had large families, which necessitated extra accommodation in the matter of schools.
Mr. SEXiSMlITH: I would ask the hon. member what large families in southern Saskatchewan have to do with the item before the Chair?

I only mentioned that incidentally when I branched into this digression from the main subject. But it has this connection with the matter under discussion: I am desirous that the Department of Agriculture should use some of this $1,200,000 to assist the farmers in these isolated places by establishing model farms to show the farmers how to operate their farms to the best advantage and to relieve the labour situation. It must be remembered that farmers come into competition for labour with manufacturing concerns. They also come into competition with the tobacco growers, who offer higher wages than the farmers can afford to offer. If you make conditions favourable for farm help they will not want to indulge in the extravagances of city life, nor will they seek rwhat the Civil Service has to offer. If you assist the farmers along the lines I suggest you wall accomplish much. I find in the bulletin a summary of the situation, and as it is not lengthy I shall read it. It appears under the heading "Labour and Wages.'' This statement reads as follows:
Farm labour conditions were never more acute, even during the latter years of the war. The rates of wages have been steadily mount-ting, and are now regarded as impossible to meet by a number of correspondents. While some farmers are seeking men at any price, others bluntly state that they will have to do with what labour they can muster at home and let the remainder of the work go.

Now, Mr. Chairman, this is undeniably a most serious condition of affairs, and in my judgment is requires the earnest, and more than that the immediate, consideration of the minister. I think it is of greater importance now to provide satisfactory labour than even to undertake the further development of stock or the production of seed. Farmers have an abundance of seed at the present time tout they need help to sow that seed, and, when the proper time comes, to harvest the crop. To continue :
Many also are " seeding down " to conserve labour.
This ds another serious situation in view of the fact that we are anxious to increase ^production.
Several correspondents point out that it is impossible for the average food producing farmer to successfully compete with manufacturers, shopkeepers, lumbermen, owners of lake vessels and even with such special crop raisers as tobacco growers and truck farmers so far as paying wages is concerned. The alluring call of urban life, with its short hours and entertaining scenes, is also referred to by correspondents. Wages for farm labourers vary greatly according to nearness to manufacturing centres and general location, and also the experience and ability of the worker. From $40 to $80 a month with board-and even higher- are quoted for single men for the summer, and from $70 to $100 a month with house, garden, milk, etc., to married men working the year round. From $3 to $4 a day with board is being offered for short-term workers.
These wages will not compete with the wages offered by manufacturers, lumbermen and others who are able to pay higher rates. This condition of affairs, Mr. Chairman, is causing unrest among the farmers, and a great many iarms are being sold in various parts of Ontario. For instance, take the county of Elgin. I find that a farmer, writing to the Department of Agriculture of Ontario, says:
Malahide, Elgin: More farms have been sold in this township during the last six months than for years before, and many of them were sold to persons who were not farmers.
Now, Sir, *this is not improving the situation very much, and if we cannot encourage capable men to take charge of valuable farms the results will be far from gratifying. Another farmer writes from Lanark:
Montague. Lanark: A number of farmers in this township say that they are not going to work fourteen or fifteen hours a day to raise provisions to feed the city man who wants an eight-hour day.
This is just the way that the farmers are thinking. From Plantagenet, South Prescott, the following comes:
We do what we can and let the rest go. Half the farms are left to be managed by men and women past their prime.
, Another farmer from Elgin writes:
Hired help are asking from $600 to $1,000 a year with house, garden, fuel, milk and what eggs they can use.
Just imagine, Mr. Chairnian! "What, eggs they can use," with eggs at present prices. Why, that would mean an enormous addition to the wages asked for. The statement goes on to say:
The farmers are few who can stand that; they might better work for the hired man. The only solution of the problem is pasture more and till less. Many farmers are selling out and moving to town.
Another man writing from Stephen, Huron, says:
Farm labour is scarce. Between $60 and $65 a month is paid to hands and horse kept. Nearly all are leaving for the cities, where they have short hours and high wages.
I will not tire the committee by reading other statements which I have in connection with this matter. The main point I desire to emphasize is that the minister would be well advised if he diverted some of the money which is being voted under this item towards inducing some help to go to the assistance of the farmers who are quite evidently very badly in need of assistance.

I rise simply for the purpose of expressing my appreciation of the admirable way in Which the Minister of Agriculture has presented the facts regarding his department. Certainly his address this afternoon was a splendid one from every point of view. It contained a great deal of valuable information and I sincerely trust that the suggestion which has been made will be carried out, and that his address will find a wider range of publicity than it will receive by being simply recorded on the pages of Hansard. I hope it will be printed in pamphlet form and distributed throughout the Dominion so that farmers in every part of the country may derive some 'real benefit from the information which it gives in such abundance. I am sure that a careful study of the minister's speech will enable the farmers to employ improved methods in their prosecution of agriculture, and I am inclined to think that the facts contained in it will be a revelation to a very large number-probably the majority-of the farmers of Canada. A perusal of the minister's speech will show them how extensive is the work carried on by the department and what ex-

cellent progress has been made in the development of agriculture. In my province there is an experimental farm, which, so far as I know, is doing good work, and I shall be extremely pleased to hear from the minister some reference to the progress which that farm is making. If it is the hope of the minister to visit the experimental farms in the various provinces I shall be delighted to learn that he will include in his itinerary the Garden of the Gulf and see how things are getting along down there. I do not think I shall trespass upon the time of the House any longer. I might perhaps have been disposed to extend my remarks somewhat farther were it not for the enormous amount of time consumed and the variety of subjects discussed and passed under review by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Ped-low).

With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for King's, P. E. I., (Mr. Mclsaac) I am glad to say that the farm at Charlottetown is making satisfactory progress. A good deal of work has been carried on in connection with crop production, poultry and steer feeding experiments. We are increasing our livestock at that farm, we are taking up dairying, hog raising and so on, and the farm is making good progress under present conditions.

I have not heard from the minister whether he intends to consider the great central part of Ontario. I am glad to hear of the splendid progress that is being made in the East and also in the West, but it seems he is overlooking the good old province of Ontario. We have in Peterborough, Victoria, Bali-9 p.m. burton, North and South Ontario, Durham, and Hastings counties a district which is not excelled for mixed farming anywhere in Canada. That high-priced calf that the minister spoke of this afternoon in his splendid address was developed in that district. We have developed, I am proud to say, in the county of Peterborough, some of the best dairy and beef herds in Canada. I have been told by the judges sent out from the department to the little agricultural fair that we hold in the village of Norwood in my riding that it is the best agricultural fair between Markham and Sherbrooke, and there is to be seen at it some of the finest dairy and beef cattle to be found anywhere in the country. We have not had any assistance from the department in the way of 
demonstration or experimental farms. I am not thinking for a minute that it is necessary to establish an experimental farm. I would not advocate or support it. Demonstration farms, as my hon. friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) said, might well be established in every county. I would be inclined to favour that. I do not see any reason why a farm of 100 or 200 acres could not be taken in every county. If an expert were put on such a farm it could be made to pay and pay well. It would be a great object lesson to the farmers in the district. I do not wish to ramble all over the Dominion talking about southern Alberta and the conditions there and all the other parts of Canada, I only wish to impress upon the minister the necessity of giving the central district of Ontario some consideration. I would like to know if it is his intention to do so.
I would like to suggest to the minister that he do not go to the expense of establishing demonstration farms throughout the counties. Why not hire the men who do the farming already?
The hon. member need not be afraid of that.

Agriculture being the basic industry of this country when anything appertaining to it is under discussion in this House, it should be given full and sympathetic consideration. I am not going to embarrass the minister with an application for an experimental farm.
Do not be bashful.

I am not bashful. My application has been in for a considerable time and I am very glad it is, in view of the fact that so many hon. gentlemen have made application to him at this time. In his splendid address this afternoon the minister spoke about increased production. I am sure if there is one thing that is engaging the attention of the thoughtful people of this country at the present time it is the matter of increased production. The minister divided the topic under two heads. First, he urged that there should be increased production from the land already under cultivation. I am sure that the minister, the officers under him and the staffs that he has upon his experimental farms, are in a position to lead the way in respect to this matter. The other point about increasing production by bringing under cultivation raw or new lands is a mat-

ter that has to be looked at from a different standpoint. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Ped-low), there is a shortage of help in this country and if we are going to bring new land under cultivation we need more help. I am sure that the minister must know that there is a real shortage of farm help in the country to-day. Before we can consider bringing any large areas of new land under cultivation it would be well to give consideration to the help problem. The minister spoke about the class of immigrants that he would like to see coming into this country in larger numbers. I am sure every member of the committee will agree that the class that he described would be very desirable immigrants if we were able to get them. But the minister did not enlighten the committee as to where he was going to get this class of immigrants. It is all very well to set up standards but in this connection beggars cannot logically at any rate be choosers. When we take into consideration that we are losing a great many of that class of our people who formerly have done the manual labour of this country I think it is well for us to consider just where to draw the line with regard to immigration.
Does the hon. gentleman mean that he would be in favour of allowing the immigration of cheap labourers into Canada?

I mean just what I
said; it would be well for the minister and the Government to give this matter serious consideration. The minister also referred to the importance of good seed and good sires There is no man who has had to do with agriculture, either growing grain or raising livestock, but will know that the advice given the committee this afternoon by the minister was good. In the province of Saskatchewan from which I come the only men who are successful in their work upon the land are those who give particular attention to intensive cultivation. To succeed in farming in Saskatchewan one must give every consideration to the cultivation of the soil. After having done this it is well to use the very best seed, and in breeding livestock to use the best sires that are procurable. The minister also mentioned the cultivation of sunflowers as silage feed. I am sure this is an important matter. We have just come through a very trying winter in the western provinces owing to a great shortage of feed, and if the growing of sunflowers will in any way help in the event
of a recurrence of such a shortage it should be given every attention by the department.
I wish to endorse what the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Wilson) said this afternoon respecting the great service rendered this country by Mr. Seager Wheeler, of Rosthern, Saskatchewan. This gentleman has brought honour not only to himself and to the province but to the whole Dominion, having on many occasions won the world's championship for wheat and the coarser grains. As pointed1 out by the hon. member for Saskatoon, the degree of LL.D. was conferred upon Mr. Wheeler a few days ago by Queen's University. I think the least the Department of Agriculture could do would be to put this gentleman in such a position that he would be relieved from the worry of making a living for himself while carrying on his experimental work. He is doing that work off his own bat, so to speak, having received no assistance from the Provincial or the Federal Government, and I think it is time the department recognized the valuable servcies that Mr. Wheeler has rendered this country.

Mr. Chairman, in regard to what the hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Sexsmith) said about the absence of an illustration station in his section of Ontario, I am very glad indeed to hear that such excellent cattle are produced there-this is not the first time I have heard of them-and also to know what a very fine quality of farming is carried on there. That is probably one of the reasons why that section has not yet received an illustration station, because no doubt the department has been careful to select those sections where the farming is not so good and illustration stations are more necessary. However, we are now taking up the matter of establishing illustration stations in Ontario, and when we come to a decision the claims of Peterborough will be given very careful consideration.
With respect to the labour situation, it is pretty bad all over this continent. I do not think we are any worse off on our farms than they are in the United States and some other parts of the world. Being one of the results of the war, it is a very difficult condition to regulate. We have established labour bureaus in various parts of the country in co-operation with the provi-incial authorities and those in charge are doing the best they can to supply men. In Western Canada, I think, conditions are a great deal better than in Ontario. This department has been in touch with the Department of Immigration, whose business it is

to take care of these matters, and they assure us that they are making a very strong effort to help out as far as they possibly can.'

Mr. Chairman, I listened with considerable pleasure to the hon. minister while he was giving us his well-thought out brief. It brought to my mind what I have often heard repeated in the last two or three years,-that we were having too many farmers in Parliament. So far, I think the record of the present Minister of Agriculture will bear out my statement that he, at any rate, is "the right man in the right place."
'He has told us of the progressive improvement of our dairy strains of cattle, which, of course, we are all glad to hear. But I think he forgot to say a word on behalf of the beef strains of cattle,-and judging from the appearence of my hon. friend I believe that he enjoys a juicy beefsteak just as much as I do. But he cannot get that delicacy from the dairy cow; it must come from the beef cattle. In that connection let me add, that I have noticed that sires are provided by the department in settlements in the West where the farmers keep only a few cows. In my opinion,-and I speak as a farmer of some experience,-the quality of the sires is not up to the standard that it should be, and I hope the minister will see to it that that standard shall be reached by the sires which are supplied from time to time. It is a good investment, and when a sire is purchased a few hundred dollars extra should not be considered if an animal of the right quality is secured.
I would like the minister to inform the committee what was the net result of a shipment of two carloads of steers sent from the West to the Experimental Farm here. I met a farmer yesterday who is farming within a short distance of the city, and he told me that at the present time it did not pay to stall beef cattle. So perhaps the minister could give us some valuable information along that line.
I was rather amused when the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) told us of his trip out West to the "isolated" constituency of Assiniboia. There can be no doubt that when he left home he had an impression that this constituency was a benighted district, but when he got there and saw that the people could build three public schools and one high school no doubt he came to the conclusion that, after all, they were not so badly "isolated." I do hope that my good friend from South Ren-

frew will again visit the West on some similar occasion and help us out.
I do not wish to press the minister at this time for an experimental or a demonstration farm in my consistuency; I think there have been too many requests of that sort already. I will wait until a more opportune time. I wish the hon. minister every success in his department and I have great hopes that he will contine to be " the right man in the right place."
Mr. 'OAH1ILL: Would the minister advise us what the intention of the Goverment is with regard to the Kapuskasing Experimental Farm?

The land was given to the department. The cost of operation last year, including buildings and clearing, was about $60,000. The buildings are nearly completed now, land we intend to operate the farm as the other farms are operated. We feel that this farm can render a valu-ble service in that clay district where the soil is somewhiat different from that of the other farms in Ontario.
Will the minister tell us something about Spirit Lake, in the province of Quebec? The experimental farm there also was built by German prisoners.

Spirit Lake is another farm that was given to us. The amount spent on it so far is not quite as great as the amount spent on Kapuskasing. We have not erected as many buildings; we have not got as far advanced as we have at Kapuskasing. But it is the intention of the Government to go ahead with the development of that farm, which is in a clay loam district.

These two farms are on the Transcontinental, in the clay belt in Northern Ontario and Quebec. In the district where the Spirit Lake farm is situated there is a settlement of from fifteen to twenty thousand people. At Spirit Lake considerable farming is under way, it is now a farming territory; but at Kapuskasing not one hundred acres of land are under cultivation, outside of the experimental farm. If my memory serves me well, a report was recently published in the press of a commission which investigated the settlement at Kapuskaisiing, and from it I understand that most of the settlers have left that territory. How much money has been spent in *the Spirit Lake territory?
, Mr. TOLMIE: I am sorry that I cannot give the hon. member the information, but I shall be glad to get it for him.
Before this item is passed?
I hardly think that the hon. member would want to hold up the item pending the furnishing of this information.

Well, this item is more important, perhaps, than the minister thinks. There is a settlement in the Spirit Lake territory, in the province of Quebec; every effort is being made to colonize it. The people there are practical farmers; they are not people who have been brought in by .any assistance, they have gone in on their own account; they are clearing the land and cultivating ft and making their homes there without assistance from the Government or from any other source. While settlers ara being carted back from the Ontario end of the Transcontinental, people are going into this other territory by the hundreds. All they want is good railway facilities and the ordinary encouragement that a Government may give. I am anxious to know wdiat money has been spent, at Spirit Lake, because Spirit Lake is much more advantageously situated so far as settlement is concerned than Kapusbasing ever will be, -at least, until there is .a different immigration and colonization policy in Ontario.
At Spirit Lake we are expending this year $45,000.
And $60,000 at Ka.puska-sing?

That was last year; it included expenditure on buildings, which will not be necessary this year.
Mr. (CAHILL: Have you in the Estimates for .this year $45,000 to be spent at Spirit Lake?
Yes.
And how much at Kapus-kasing?
The amount is $56,000. There is a very much larger area of land to be cleared at Kapuskasing.

Doeis the minister think that Kapuskasing is the proper place to develop, to .the detriment of the Spirit Lake territory? Does he think it is necessary to have two experimental farms in such close proximity to each other in that northern country? Would it not be better to spend all the money in one farm and have that farm do some good?

I have never visited Kapuskasing, but I am informed that the land is of good quality and that we can look
forward to considerable development there, Spirit Lake i.s also a promising district.

The minister is correctly informed. There is nothing wrong with the territory; the land is good enough. If the territory were colonized the Transcontinental railway would serve a good purpose. But until the Ontario Government have some system of colonization, or will allow the only class of people who will ever settle that northern country to go in there, it is absolutely foolish for the Dominion Government to be spending money (in ia territory where you are mot going 'to get settlers. And I repeat 'that under the present system of colonization iin Ontario you will not get settlers in that country.
What has happened since the German prisoners went away? Who has been working the land at Spirit Lake?
We have a superintendent there and a number of men.
How many men?
About twenty.

Before the discussion
of this interesting subject comes to a close I should like to ask a question that seems to me to be quite pertinent. There are at the present time, when these most important Estimates are being considered, less than thirty members in the Chamber. It has been the same every year while I have been in the House; almost without exception the Farmer members pay no attention at all to the Agriculture Estimates. Look at the Farmers' party over there!
How many are there?

The hon. gentleman
who is the sole occupant of the cross benches at this moment (Mr. Andrews) is a distinguished soldier; I do not know that he is a distinguished farmer. But every other member of the Farmers' party-except the one who has come in just now, at an opportune moment (Mr. Johnston)-is an absentee. That is the interest that the members of the Farmers' party take in the farming affairs of this country. It is not because they have any criticism to make, because one of their members said a few minutes ago that the Minister of Agriculture was the right man in the right place. They have no criticism to make; they have no suggestions to offer; yet they are a Farmers' party.

That is why they
went out; they have no criticism to make.

I see that my hon.
friend does not know anything about agriculture. Speaking for that large class of people who are more or less ignorant of agriculture, I think that the farmers in this House might do the Test of the population of this country the honour, if they will not do the farming community the justice, of staying on the scene and giving their best thought and consideration to the Estimates of the Minister of Agriculture when they come year after year. I am glad to see that at this moment the distinguished leader of the Farmers' party (Mr.	Crerar) has come in.
We now have a total of three in the Farmers' party, hut the best part of the Agriculture Estimates and the discussion on them is over. After hearing so much about the labour question, I should like to ask the leader of the Farmers' party what he proposes to do about labour. I asked the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) if he proposed to admit cheap labour into this country. He, of course promptly fenced the question and returned me a sharp, but not an explanatory answer. I should like, and we should all like to know how this question of labour is going to be solved. Farmers, I understand, rebel against working fourteen hours a day-as they do in summer, but not in winter- whilst people in towns work eight hours or, perhaps, nine hours a day. The conditions are different. The people who have been on the farm do not want to stay there; they want to leave the farm. What we would like to know is, how the farming community and the leader of the Farmers' party propose to remedy the-situation; because we can possibly assist him, and we shall do our best to do so. But is the situation to be remedied by the employment of cheap labour or by simply throwing down the barriers and allowing everything to come in at its cheapest from China and other parts of the world? I know the hon. member (Mr. Cahill) would let anything at all come into this country. He does not care about the farmers of Quebec or the manufacturers; it is cheapness he wants. I believe, however, the leader of the Farmers' party is a different type of man, and I am sure on this matter he would be pleased to give us the benefit of his experience.

I cannot think the
hon. member was serious in his criticism of members of this group for non-attendance in this chamber. I am sure every hon. member of the House must know that these

benches have been well filled during all the discussion on the Estimates that have been before the committee. He complained because I did not give an answer to his question regarding the class of immigrants to be admitted to this country. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that, the help problem of this country is one for the Government to consider, not for me.

I should like to ask the
minister again if he would not consider amalgamating those two farms to which I have referred and putting them where they would be useful, instead of spending fifty or sixty thousand dollars at a point where there is no settlement and where there seems to be little possibility of settlement in the near future. It seems that after we start an experiment, we must	continue spending money endlessly	with apparently	no	object
in view. The minister himself states that he has not visited that section of the country and that he knows nothing about the territory, but that it is reported to him as good territory. The territory is all right, but an experimental farm in a section where there is no settlement and where there is another experimental farm a few miles away with a settlement around it seems unnecessary. It would be better to spend the money where you have a settlement than to spend money in a part of the country where you have no hope of settlement in the near future. Unless you are spending money to some advantage, an item of $50.000 is worthy of consideration. The item seems to keep on growing from year to year, and I think the minister would do well to strike out that appropriation of $50,000 this year. If it is necessary to spend it somewhere else, do so, but I would not ask the minister to spend it at Spirit Lake.
How far apart are these two farms?
Why expend more money there than in other districts where there is settlement?
Because we have a very much larger plant there, and necessarily there is a call for more money.
Why put a larger plant there when there is no settlement?
The plant was there before I was here.
It was not there before the Government of which my hon. friend is a member was here.
It's a war baby.

I am informed that it was there before this Government was in power at all.
Branch of Entomology, $18,000.
I should like the minister to\ give some explanation of what entomology is.

It is the study of parasites as affecting agriculture. It is a very important work. It is estimated that these parasites cause a loss every year in Canada of $125,000,000. We have a staff of entomologists who make a study of the life history of these parasites and of the various insecticides that can be used to destroy them, and the securing of cheap insecticides. Some of the big problems they are engaged on at the present time are the grasshopper plague on the prairies, the mosquitoes in the raspberry growing section of British Columbia, and the browntailed moth.

As I understand the minister's explanation, it sounds like the ward heelers attached to the Union Government.
For the administration and enforcement of the Destructive Insect and Pest Act, $150,000.
What progress is being made with this?

We are making some progress with the grasshopper plague out in Western Canada. As I pointed out this afternoon, it will require about 2,000 tons of bran, nearly 100,000 pounds of arsenic, and 50,000 gallons of syrup to make a bait to scatter around the grasshopper districts with a view to destroying them. We are also carrying on a mosquito investigation in the Fraser River valley, where the mosquitoes have been so bad as to drive away the pickers in the raspberry and strawberry districts during the harvesting season. We are also working on the pear thrip, a parasite that attacks the pear orchards. On Vancouver Island a harvest of only 700 boxes was obtained from an orchard one year owing to this parasite, but after the entomologists had studied the problem and their recommendations had been carried out 7,000 boxes were obtained the next year. We are also working on the spruce bud moth, and another parasite affecting the bark of the fir trees in British Columbia, and we expect excellent results from these investigations. We are also working on the brown-tailed moth in the Maritime Provinces and at the present time have just about eliminated it. The life history of these parasites has to be carefully studied to enable us to adopt the proper methods to counteract them. We are also studying how to get cheap tree sprays to he used in the large orchard districts of the Niagara 	1
valley, the Annapolis valley and British Columbia. The work the entomologists are doing is a very valuable one.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Power) raised the question as to what the study of entomology was. Perhaps he would pardon me if I gave him a little illustration of its value, which is pretty well known to anybody who has given any study to the subject. Borne years ago the citrus fruit industry-the orange, lemon and grape fruit industry-of California, which has an output of probably $100,000,000 a year, was threatened by an invasion of the orchards by an insect called the cottony cushion-scale, belonging to an order of insects which live on the sap of trees. No remedy was found for a long time, and it looked as if the whole industry was threatened with extinction. Then several of the best entomologists were put to work on the problem, and after a long time one of the entomological experts travelling in Australia to try and find out where this particular cottony cushion-scale came from, and what particular insect preyed on it, thereby keeping it in check, discovered that it was indigenous to Australia, and that these insects were kept down in numbers by being lived upon as a food by a particular species of beetle belonging to the so-called lady bird family. When this entomologist discovered that this lady bird or lady beetle fed on the cottony cushion-scale, thereby keeping the pest in check and rendering it non-injurious to vegetation, thousands and thousands of these beetles were imported into California, and they went on breeding there until in the course of three or four years they had bred to such an extent that they had practically wiped out the cottony cushion-scale in California, and saved the citrus industry, which represents an investment of untold millions of dollars. I think that is about as good an illustration as can be given of the economic value of entomology in a hundred different lines.
Before taking my seat I should like to pay my personal tribute, as Minister of Agriculture in the past, occupying the position which my hon. friend (Mr. Tolmie) does now, to the work of a very capable entomologist in the service of the Dominion Government, who, I regret to say lately died. I refer to the late Dr. Gordon C. Hewitt, who by his work in this particular branch ,of the service conferred enormous benefits not only upon the department but upon the whole country.

For the development of the dairying industry, and the improvement of transportation, sale and trade in food and other products, $165,000.

I think this is one of the fields in which there is duplication by the Provincial and Federal Governments. To my knowledge, work along this line is being done by the province of Quebec. I should be glad if the minister would let us know what is being done along federal lines.

The Dominion Government's work in this connection consists in the promoting of dairying generally. We also carry on cow testing associations in cooperation with the Provincial Governments. We carry on improvements in the manufacture of butter and cheese through instruction; provide plans for dairy buildings; and make investigations of special problems in dairying. We operate a station at Finch, Ontario, for demonstration purposes. The Dominion Government also carry out the oleomargarine regulations, and cargo inspection at Candian and United Kingdom ports. We have several inspectors overseas who inspect cargoes on their arrival in order to keep us fully informed concerning their condition when they reach the other side, and enable us to provide that the goods may reach the consumer in the best possible shape. We also handle a refrigerator car service for both butter and cheese; we attend to cold storage and pre-cooling of fruit, and carry on fruit storage investigations. We are conducting some interesting investigations this year in connection with the storage of fruit and the shipping of fruit in refrigerator cars, and we expect from these investigations to obtain some very valuable information. We carry out the administration of the Gold Storage Act and the Cold Storage Warehouse Act, as well as the regulations in regard to creameries. We issue monthly a dairy news letter, and weekly a dairy produce market report; and in connection with the proposed new work we intend to take up scientific dairy research, which is something that has not hitherto been done in this country. We also deal with cheese factory and creamery economics. The Provincial Government do a great deal of educational work but there is no real clashing between the two departs ments. We co-operate with the provincial dairy departments wherever it is possible to do so and we render every assistance we can, feeling that Qur objective is the same as that of the provinces.

The minister's statement
would tend to confirm the assertion of the 153
hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) this afternoon that improvement is possible in the way of avoiding duplication in the work done by the Federal and the Provincial Governments. Item 45 is divided into two parts, the first referring to development of the dairying industry and the second providing for the improvement of transportation, sale and trade in food and other products. I understand that the latter belongs to the Federal Government. But the first part of the item in regard to the development of the dairying industry seems to me to appertain more particularly to the Provincial Governments, and I asked the question which I did because it appeared to me that there was useless duplication in the work accomplished by the Dominion Government on the one hand and the Provincial Governments on the other.
There is no serious duplication at all.

I am glad to learn that
fact.

What method is employed by the Government to bring to the attention of the individual farmer the information obtained from the dairy records? Is there any special method that enables the department to have that information completely disseminated? I quite appreciate the fact that there are many farmers who are alive to the value of dairy records and cow testing and who seek information because they are interested. But that is the class of farmer who needs information least; he is alive and up-to-date. There is the other man, however, who probably lives alongside the energetic farmer, and it is of him that I am speaking. What is done to buoy him up and to induce him to take a keener interest in the improvement of his own herd?

How many copies of the Agricultural Gazette would reach individuals in the riding which T have the honour



to represent, lor instance? Is there a list on which the names of persons who might need the Agricultural Gazette or the dairy news letter could he enrolled?

This information is sent
to those people who apply for it. It is an expensive matter to distribute material of this kind indiscriminately throughout the country because in many cases it is only thrown aside. It is not deemed wise to send it to those who do not ask for it. In all cases in which the bulletins are asked for they are sent, because the very fact that there is a demand for them shows that the farmers to whom they are sent are interested. In all such cases we are glad to send all the information we have.
Do I understand that all the names that might be sent in by a member of the House would be put on a list and that those persons would become regular receivers of the Agricultural Gazette?

Not of the Agricultural
Gazette, but of the bulletins. We shall be glad to furnish them with those.'
Would that include the dairy news letter?
If they wish it.
What did the transportation which is included in this item amount to last year?
I may point out to the hon. member that we do not pay any transportation; we simply supervise the transportation of shipments.
The item is "improvement of transportation." What does that mean?

We are continually seeking methods by which transportation can be improved. For instance, we are carrying on some experiments this year through an arrangement with the railway companies and the fruit men, making a test in regard to the recording of temperatures in refrigerator ears, etc., and we trust that a good deal of valuable information will be secured. 'Shipments are also pre-cooled before they are put into the refrigerator cars, and the temperature is carefully noted. These experiments are being conducted this summer at the request of a large number of fruit men and we expect that beneficial results will be derived from them. In connection with refrigerator car inspection and 
market reporting last year the expenditure was $3,570. This covers refrigerator car inspection at Montreal and Toronto.
In regard to the establishment of a station at Finch for the improvement of the cheese industry, I should like to know exactly what is being done in this direction.

We have taken hold of two cheese factories at Finch and are operating them as model factories. Any man who wishes to learn anything about the cheese and butter business can go there and see how things are done in an up-to-date way. It has proved of great value to the cheese makers. We are making cheese and butter and shipping milk, and the station has been showing a profit.
Where is the station?
About fifty miles south between here and Cornwall.

I suppose it is well recognized that in a district such as I have the honour to represent, and in other districts, this country produces a tremendous lot of what we ordinarily call factory cheese. That is a cheese of 75 or 80 pounds. This cheese is practically all shipped out of the country because Canadians do not appear to be a cheese-consuming people. I fancy it is safe to say that from $25,000,000 to $30,000,000 worth'of cheese is exported annually. It is a strange thing that the Canadian public will not eat cheese to anything like what may be deemed a reasonable extent. People eat a little cheese but not much. The British consuming public seem to eat more cheese, especially if they can get a glass of beer with it. In the absence of that trade in this country have the Government ever considered the idea that there must be a tremendous quantity of cheese that is imported from other countries such as Roquefort, Gorgonzola, Edam and other varieties that before the war at any rate were brought in here and sold at from GO cents to 75 cents a pound? I believe that to-day Roquefort will cost $2 a pound. This condition exists while there are a lot of districts in this country with the finest pasturage in the world and cows that stand up equal to those in any other place because the farmers and dairymen have made great strides in developing, through pure-bred sires, valuable herds. Yet there is no incentive apparently given to the people to go in for a finer and smaller package kind of cheese outside of the

factory at Ingersoll. That is
10 p.m. about the only place where they
.	put up some small packages of
pimento and ordinary cheese. On the general argument that the home market in everything else is the best for the farmer, it ought to be the best for the cheese farmer -the man who develops and uses his farm largely for dairy purposes.
