I throw it out as a suggestion to the minister that if this factory at Finch is only dealing with and putting forward to the people of Ontario the production of what is called cheddar cheese, or some such name, there might be a great opening for the Government to establish at that factory the manufacture of a small cheese of the richer variety which, if this production were extended to the country districts under proper educational facilities, would induce capital among the farming body to be invested on the co-operative plan, to establish factories in the dairy centres which would supply a cheese that the people of Canada would eat and that also would give a better remuneration. I would ask the minister to look into that.

We have been making a
few of the small cheddar cheese at Finch. I shall be very glad indeed to accept the suggestion of the hon. member and look into the matter further.

This item is perhaps one of the most important in the Estimates we have under consideration. I might say with reference to the point raised by the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) that we have several varieties of cheese made in Canada other than the Canadian cheddar which is sold in Great Britain. We have the Oka cheese made by the Trap-pist, the Experimental Farm cream cheese, and several other varieties of that kind. I believe the hon. gentleman will find quite a sufficient variety to satisfy his taste in that respect. But apart from that, our cheese industry in Canada is undoubtedly one of the important branches of our agricultural industry. Canada has for many years occupied a pre-eminent place in the British market for her cheese products and the total exports have run from 175,000,000 to 200,000,000 pounds per year. I am confident that we can establish a similar preeminence in respect to our butter output. In building up this industry, however, the question of transportation and particularly of modern refrigeration as applied to transportation is of the highest importance. I think that any money that is expended in 1534
the way of improved transporation facilities and in the way of finding out the best methods of refrigeration and of handling these commodities will certainly be money well spent. We should not overlook the fact that our position in Canada is a very favourable one in respect to the world's markets. We have heard from the minister already about the position which our cheese occupies in the British market. There is no reason why our butter should not occupy an equally favourable position. We have in addition to that a vast and growing market immediately to the south which is bound in the years to come to lake large quantities of our dairy products. The fact is sometimes overlooked that more than half of the population of the United States lies east of a line drawn north and south through Chicago. By far the most densely populated portion of the United States, within twelve or fifteen hours by train from one of the finest agricultural parts of this Dominion, namely the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. If we have vision to look into the future we have a splendid prospect ahead of us in respect to the development of our dairy industry. I say again that any assistance we can give in the direction of perfecting the methods of transportation and particularly the development of proper cold storage facilities, so that these commodities that- are of a perishable character can be brought to the markets in the best condition, will' be money well spent. It is now generally recognized particularly with respect to food products of this class, that quality is of the highest consideration and if we can make cheese and butter of the highest quality and can get proper facilities for taking them to the markets of the world in the best possible shape, the dairy farmers of Eastern Canada particularly-because they are more favourably situated in that regard than the dairy farmers of the rest of Canada- can find a ready and profitable market for everything they can produce.	.
Has the minister considered adopting a policy whereby fertilizers can be obtained at or as near cost as possible by those engaged in the dairying and other branches of agricultural industry?

We fully realize the value of getting fertilizers to the farmers at the very lowest possible cost, but, as the hon. gentleman will understand, railway rates are very high and concessions are very difficult to get.

It is because railway rates are so high that I aim anxious to know if the Government has any policy on this matter. It is one of the most important considerations, I imagine, in connection with agriculture that fertilizers should be obtainable by our farmers at the minimum cost; and it seems to me that because we have these high transportation charges the Government ought to formulate o poliev to deal with the matter.
I am glad the hon. gentleman has brought this matter to my attention. I will look into it further.
What instructions are the government milk testers given in regard' to their duties and their districts?

These cow testers are directly under the; control of the Provincial Governments as to their [particular districts, but we have certain men who go out among the farmers and interest them in the advantages of cow testing. These tests are of great value to the dairyman, because it is the only method iby which he can tell the best cows in his herd, the Teal test, of course, being the Ibutter-fat content rather than fine looks, and he is thus enabled to eliminate his poor cows. The men we send out arrange with the cheesemaker or butter-maker, as the case may be, connected with the local creamery to test the milk, and we pay the tester.
Is it his duty to test oniy the milk of the patrons of the factory, or is he instructed to test any cow in the district?
He is instructed to test any cow throughout the district.

I have personal knowledge of one case where a farmer, not a patron of the local butter factory, sent his milk to be tested, but a month or two afterwards the testing officer said that he would not test the milk of any farmers outside the patrons of the factory. That is the reason for my 'question.
If the hon. member will be good enough to bring the case to the attention of the department, we will be very glad to get a report on it and take any action that may be necessary.

I do not wish to delay tha Estimates for more than a minute or two. but I was rather interested in the remarks of the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) and the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) regarding cheese. I

know very little about cheesemaking, but for some years I have been more or less of an epicure in regard to cheese, and I w.as struck by the remarks of the hon. member for North Perth when he drew the attention of the committee to our cheese production. I think those remarks are well worthy of careful consideration by the minister, who has given us such a very excellent report this afternoon and has shown such a high quality of management in his department. A short time ago the hon. member for Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards) told us that the province of Quebec had the finest record in this country for the quality of its butter, and I think I would be quite safe in saying that the province has an equally fine record both as to the quality and variety of its cheese production, and I was a little surprised that some hon. member from that province did not rise to confirm that statement.
The point I wish to make is that we are to-day producing, especially in the province of Quebec, cheese which is quite equal-and I think I am a fair judge as an eater of cheese-to any of the imported European varieties, such as Roquefort and iGamem-bert. The only trouble is that our fine varieties, such as the Oka, the Trappist and the Beloeil are not made in large quantities, in fact, we cannot begin to supply the demand. The cheese from Beloeil is made by two or three farmers there, it has a most delicious flavour, but so far as I know it has never reached the markets beyond Ottawa. I have purchased it many times in this city, and have taken it to my home a thousand miles west, and every one who has tasted it has passed the most complimentary remarks regarding its quality and flavour.
I think it would be well for the minister and his deputy to consider the advisability of encouraging the making of this delicious cheese which the province of Quebec excels in producing. In the European markets when any one is buying cheese he considers our ordinary Canadian cheese of very superior quality-and we know it has a high food value-but in addition a very well-known cheese is sold as "old" Canadian cheese, and that cheese when properly cured is, to my mind, almost equal to any Roquefort we import. Therefore, I think the production of old Canadian Cheese-which I presume is simply our ordinary cheese aged for a certain time-of Oka, of Trappist and of Beloeil cheese, should be heartily encouraged by the minister and his depart-

rnent, for the reason that those varieties might well take the place to a certain extent of the expensive cheeses imported from Europe. I merely wish to offer that suggestion by way of supplementing the remarks of the hon. member for Perth and the hon. member for Marquette.

I thank the minister for his kindness in promising to look further into the question of the transportation of fertilizers. In that connection may I say one word as representing one of the Prince Edward Island constituencies? As the minister is aware, the products of Prince Edward Island are almost exclusively agricultural, and in the province are found very rich deposits of mussel mud which is excellent as a fertilizer, but owing to the high cost of transportation those deposits are very little used. If this form of fertilizer were extensively used the agricultural products of the Island would be very considerably increased, and I would be pleased if the minister would make a point of paying particular attention to the needs of the Island in that regard. That is only one instance. I think the question of supplying fertilizers to farmers at the lowest possible transportation cost is one that might well constitute a policy which the Government should take up for the entire Dominion.

A year or two ago I communicated with the Government railways in an effort to secure a reduction in the freight rate on fertilizer that is being used in the district of Joliette in connection with the growing of tobacco. Generally speaking, i't seems to me, i't should fee the policy of the Government to make effective a general reduction of freight rates on fertilizers all over the country. The more production there is on the farm the more freight there will be for the railways; for each carload of fertilizer that the railways transport, they will receive two or three, sometimes more, carloads of agricultural product^. It has been said time and again *that railroads have been duplicated in Canada; that we have three transcontinental railroads when we should have not more than two, and so on. There is a great deal of truth in all that, and the only possible way for us to make these railroads pay is to feed them. We feed them by bringing about more agricultural production. This is a very important question for the Government to consider. If the freight rates on fertilizers were generally reduced, the result would be a benefit to the farmer,
a benefit to the railroads themselves, and a benefit to the country.
Towards the encouragement of cold storage warehouses for the better preservation and handling of perishable food products, $25,000.

Some weeks ago a delegation came here from Nova Scotia, consisting of the Provincial Secretary of Agriculture and some of his officers, to pres^ npon the Government the importance of providing cold storage facilities for export shipments of agricultural products from the Maritime Provinces. Will the minister say if the matter has been considered, and if so what decision has been reached?

At that time a committee was formed to act with the minister in looking into -this matter. We have been investigating the matter through ouir livestock branch with ia view Ito ascertaining just what supply of cattle there would be for such a plant in the Maritime Provinces. It would be necessary of course, for us to have a sufficient supply of cattle before a plant could be built and conducted at a profit, particularly with an abattoir. The report which I have from the Livestock Commissioner does not indicate that sufficient cattle would be available just now to keep such a plant going. But we are developing to the very best of our ability a co-operative selling plant whereby farmers are encouraged to form co-operative selling associations so that their cattle can be shipped in carload lobs, both to Montreal and down into the markets to the South. We hope that by following that policy for a while the supply of livestock in my hon. friend's section of the country will be so increased that it will be sufficient to maintain an abattoir. We have also taken the matter up with the Canadian National Railways and they have the whole subject under consideration. I assure the hon. member that we shall do all we possibly can to get such a plant established. It is a necessity for the farmers in his district, because at present they are very much at the mercy of the buyers. It is the same old story of the Western Canada cattle ranches; you have to Sell your cattle in the fall when they are fat, whereas if you had cold istorage 'facilities you would he able to put your beef in 'there and keep it until you could get a satisfactory price.

A year ago, if I remember correctly, an appropriation was asked for the erection of a cold storage warehouse in

Montreal. Can itlhe minister say what progress has been made, if any?
That plant is under construction, under the direction of the Harbour Commission.
Would the minister give us some general idea of the purpose of this vote?

I think that the Minister of Marine, in his usual way of getting things shoved off on somebody else, told me the other night that he had nothing to do with cold storage establishments; that they come under the Department of Agriculture. Now that both the Minister of Marine and the Minister of Agriculture are here, I wish to state that I want to get a cold storage plant for bait down in Cape Breton; which of the hon. gentlemen it comes from does not make the slightest difference. The people of that part of the country are suffering very much from want of cold storage for bait. I want to make a serious statement to the minister. In the spring of the year large quantities of small fish travel round the coast. They are not much good for food, but they make splendid bait. But the fishermen have no place to put that bait where it can be preserved; the consequence is that when the. schools of fish go by, that supply of bait disappears. Then in the fall, in September, October and on until Christmas, there is splendid cod fishing along the shores, but the difficulty is that the fishermen have no bait. The proper policy would be to have cold storage plants at certain convenient points along the shore to store the bait, and sell it. The fishermen do not want this bait for nothing; they are willing to pay for it, but they are not wealthy enough to have cold storage facilities themselves. If cold storage plants were supplied with compet-
[M, Crerar.]
ent officers in charge of them and enough was charged for the bait to cover the running expenses, that would be satisfactory. In Newfoundland, I understand, they have not only cold storage warehouses, but steamers supplying the fishermen at different points with bait out of cold storage at certain seasons of the year when they could not get it otherwise. Although we .perhaps could not put a boat on the service as is done in Newfoundland, at different points, not only Cape Breton, but all along the coast from Yarmouth to Cape North, there is great necessity for facilities of this kind. I, therefore, urge, not only upon the minister, but upon the Government generally, the great necessity for providing the facilities for which I am asking. At this season of the year millions of pounds of that bait could be caught and conserved; but when there is no way of preserving it, the opportunity is lost; and when great profits could be made by fishermen, you find the fishermen sitting on the shore on a beautiful fishing day with the fish in millions around them, but unable to catch the fish because they have no bait. This is the actual condition of things, and I am not exaggerating. When I appealed to the department before, I was told that there was a certain company at Canso which had some bait stored away, tout the company said: Our bait is for ourselves; the storage is our own, and we are not going to give our bait to others. The result was that the fishermen had to go without it. Possibly with some exertion those fishermen might manage to get a place for themselves, but that would take a considerable amount of money, more than the fishermen have.
Mr. TOLMIE,:	This department has no
control over any of those bait cold storage plants. I presume if some of the bait was shipped to any of the plants in which we are interested, it would be accepted for storage. I realize the importance of what the hon. member says as regards having a supply of bait on hand, and I shall be glad to look further into the matter. I have not very full information at present beyond what the hon. member has given me.

Is it the Government's policy to grant these subsidies only to warehouses that are erected under the control of some municipal or other public body, or are subsidies granted sometimes to private individuals?

At the present time, only to municipalities. The subsidies were cancelled about the beginning of the war, and

I understand no subsidies have been given since.

Does the minister think that is the wisest course to [DOT]pursue? Is it not advantageous to encourage these cold storage places to as large an extent as possible?
Mr. TO'LMIE: It may 'be possible to look into this matter again with a view to taking up the subsidizing of cold storage warehouses in the near future, but up to the present I have not had an opportunity of going fully into that aspect of the case.

I have had
some correspondence with the minister as regards a cold storage warehouse at Ellers-lie, P.E.I. If the minister is looking further into the matter, I should be deeply obliged if he would give some consideration to the people of that particular part of the island. In that connection, there is one representation which I should like to bring to the minister's attention from some of the residents of Ellerslie. They point out, in connection with the cold storage warehouse there, that the company have space not only for storing what is necessary for the public needs, but for storing what is necessary for food for the fox industry. The company seem to be under the impression that because they were supplying space for food for the fox industry, they were thereby losing the opportunity of getting the Government subsidy which would go only to concerns that were supplying public needs generally. The company contend that they are endeavouring to meet those needs, and as regards the fox industry they make an interesting representation which I think is important. This is a letter I have received from two electors in Ellerslie:
We think the fox industry should have some recognition from the Federal Government, because we believe the Government will receive more income tax from the profits of fox farming than from any other source in this province, and without some means of preserving the food, this industry cannot advance as it otherwise would. If the authorities would reconsider this matter I know they would find out the advantage it would he to the Government to encourage the fur farming industry, which they would he doing, as well as giving valuable assistance to the farmers of this and the surrounding sections by giving a reasonable grant to assist the above-named organization in the erection of their chemical freezing plant.
That seems to be a practical, although a somewhat novel suggestion. The minister will realize that an industry such as the fox industry lias become in Prince Edward Island is one that it would be well
for the Government to help even in this indirect method.
Is it fish bait they feed the foxes or what?
I shall have to ask the Minister of Agriculture to answer that question as I am not an expert on the fox industry.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to what the hon. member has said regarding the storing of food for foxes, and this is a matter that might perhaps be looked into a little further. We have not neglected the fox industry altogether. We now have an expert in Prince Edward Island making a very careful study of fox diseases, that work being carried on under the Health of Animals Branch. Another department of the Government is looking into the nutrition of foxes. Fox food down there consists very largely of old horses and meat of that kind, any cheap meat the people can get hold of. I just wish to point out that we have not neglected the industry; we are taking a keen interest in it, and we are anxious indeed to assist any of these young industries that are trying to get a footing and that show prospects of succeeding.

On further reflection, I remember visiting some of the fox ranches, and one of the things that came forcibly to my notice was the quality of the food these little animals were getting. I was told that to get the better classes of furs, they sometimes feed the foxes with the very best class of meat. If that be the case, if the minister can help along the storage of the food that is necessary, he will be furthering an industry that is already one of the most important, certainly on the Island, if not in the Dominion, and one that may become of increasing importance in the -whole Dominion.

Personally, I have not a great deal of use for subsidies of any kind, and I think the subsidising of private cold storage plants in this country can now very well be discontinued. As the minister has stated, we have given in assistance in this direction something like $700,000. In many cases the result was that the government of the country contributed 30 or 33 per cent of the cost of erecting a cold storage plant, and after the subsidy was earned, the cold storage plant was used entirely for the convenience of the company that promoted and built it, and the benefits to the general public were very slight. There are

in this country cases where private cold storage companies operating in perishable commodities have been able, through the control of cold storage, to exercise a very considerable influence on the price at which they sold their commodities. Cold storage is a thing that might very well be municipally developed, and in cases where a cold storage plant is erected in this way and any merchant or dealer can secure his allotment of space, I think the department might very well be warranted in giving assistance; but the giving of assistance for the development of cold storage plants for private companies, who, after they have earned the subsidy utilize the storage entirely for their own benefit, is a different matter, and I do not think the count ry would be warranted in expending more money in that direction.
The fox industry in Prince Edward Island is a growing industry, and I have no doubt a very profitable one in view of the rising price of fum If I might offer a suggestion to the leader of the Opposition CMr. Mackenzie King) it would be this, that the fox farmers might very well practise and apply the principles of co-operation in respect to supplying themselves with the necessary storage facilities and that sort of thing for the carrying on of their industry, which the farmers of Western Canada have successfully practised in respect to the selling of grain. Self-help is the best kind of help, and if a group of farmers engaged in the fur-producing industry can get together and provide the facilities that are necessary to them in common for the carrying on of the industry, it is infinitely better for them and infinitely better for the country, than if that is done through government assistance. In the development of sound co-operative enterprise in my judgment is 'found the safest'road for the development of an industry, as well as the development of self-reliance and confidence on the part of those engaged in it.
Fruit Branch, $140,000.

Perhaps the minister
would give us an explanation of the increase in this item.

The increase is due largely to increased cost of transportation for employees, and partly to the facilities that I have already referred to regarding cold storage and the shipment of fruit under cold storage conditions.
Health of animals, $500,000.

Some time ago I was making inquiry about the shipment of cattle from the port of North Sydney to Newfoundland and other points. We have no veterinary inspector at North Sydney, and I understand that before these cattle are permitted to be put on board ship, they must be inspected. There is a veterinary at Sydney, a very competent man, but Sydney is seventeen miles away from us by land and five miles by water. The port of North Sydney is open very much later in the year than Sydney, and open earlier in the spring; so boats come round to North Sydney for loads of cattle. At present the inspector has to come seventeen miles from Sydney to do the inspecting, and that has been found very inconvenient. I do not want to interfere in any way with Dr. Thurston's employment or his salary. iHe is a returned soldier and a deserving man in every sense, but I think he has enough to do in the great city of Sydney and the town of Glace Bay and other places where he works for the Government, and as we have a veterinary in the town of North Sydney I think it would be better if a man who was right pn the spot, and who could immediately inspect these cattle, was appointed. It is very inconvenient to have to wait for this inspection, sometimes the steamers are held up, and at other times they will not wait. I have been trying to get this difficulty remedied for some time by having an inspector located at the port of North Sydney.

I am glad my hon. friend has brought that to my attention. I understand, however, that the shipments from there are very small, and that it would hardly pay to maintain a man on a salary at that point, but we might look into the advisability of having a local man do what inspecting is required and pay him by fees. I will make a note of it and see what can be done.

The shipments are not so very small. The Railway Department, after a good deal of fighting, have put up very large sheds and provided proper accommodation for the protection of these cattle. I would like to see the man who does this work paid properly, and I am sure it would not cost so very much. I am not asking that he be given a fixed salary, but it could be so arranged that he would be paid for every shipment he examined. The. veterinary in North Sydney, Mr. George Coleman, would be able to do this work very well, if the minister would make an arrangement with him. I am speaking

more in the interest of the trade than in the interest of any individual who might be appointed, but I should be very glad to see this young doctor appointed as inspector there. He is a college graduate and he could do the work very well. I am sure the minister could make an arrangement with him that would not be very expensive and that would facilitate shipments very much.
For the administration and enforcement of the Meat and Canned Foods Act, $520,000.

Why is this not under
the Department of Health? I see on the next page, by item No. 61, that the administration of the Act regarding fertilizers, is under the Department of Health. I think these two items should be transposed.

We are expecting to take
over the administration of the Act respecting fertilizers at a very early date. With regard to the inspection of meat and canned foods, these are products of the farm. The meats are slaughtered in abattoirs under the inspection of veterinarians by the Health of Animals Branch. This is one of the branches of the Agricultural Department. I think it is quite proper that the inspection should be under the Department of Agriculture, because in the first place we are dealing with agricultural products, and secondly, the work is carried out by a profession that is very closely allied with agricultural matters.
What is the explanation of the increase in this item?
It is explained by the increasing volume of business, and by the fact that we have had to engage more men to carry on this work.
I notice by the Auditor General's Report that the amount spent on this work last year was $360,836.49. An increase to $520,000 appears to me very large.
I think my hon. friend is giving the figures for the year before last.
That is correct. Is the Government receiving any return from the enforcement of this Act, or is it all expenditure and no revenue?

In carrying on the inspection of these meats we are rendering service to the whole public. We have to meet competition from the United States and the Argentine in the markets of Great Britain. In the United States this inspection is paid for by the Government. In our packing houses the packers pay for the overtime. If
they keep an inspector for three or four horns or oblige him to work on a holiday, they pay the extra charge. When this matter was under discussion a little while ago, we came to the conclusion, after an investigation, that it would not be judicious to place the packers in this country at a disadvantage in competing with the United States, the Argentine and Great Britain.
International Institute of Agriculture, to assist in maintenance thereof and to provide for representation thereat, $10,000.
Will the minister explain this item?

This is our contribution to the International Institute of Agriculture at Rome. This institute has its headquarters at Rome, and its object is to gather information in regard to agriculture from various parts of the world. By subscribing to it we aTe able to keep in close touch with the world's agriculture and to apply the information which we receive in that way toi the benefit of the farmers in this country.
Mr. MiORPHY: Who is in charge of that institute?

Mr. Doherty is the Canadian representative.
For the development of the livestock industry. $900,000.

I think it is understood that the minister would allow two or three items to remain over for discussion on a subsequent occasion. There are only a couple of items of his Estimates left now and I think he might let them stand.
If we let one stand it would serve your purpose.
I think my hon. friend had Ibetter hold this one; it is one of the largest.

Very well.
To enforce the Seed Act, to test seed for farmers and seed merchants, to encourage the production and use of superior seeds and to encourage the production of farm and garden crops, $225,000.
There is an increase of $25,000 here; perhaps the minister would explain the reason.

We have opened a new
seed laboratory in Winnipeg, and there are also increased expenses that are affecting all departments this year. This is perhaps one of the most important branches in the whole department. I think I explained

this afternoon that it handled seed during the war through what is known as the Seed Commission created to meet the situation during the war period. It handled over $12,000,000 worth of business, showing a small profit on running expenses.
